THE CORE IDEA

runs.text: A monopolist compares marginal revenue with marginal cost to choose output, then reads the corresponding price from demand. In the displayed interior solution, MR exceeds MC before their crossing and falls below MC afterward. The output decision and the price decision are separate; marginal cost need not always slope upward.

WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING MONOPOLY PRICE

runs.text: Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D slopes down from price 60 at quantity 0 to zero at 120. MR slopes down more steeply, reaching zero at 60. At quantity 40, MR and rising MC meet at 20; demand is at 40 and ATC at 45, with dashed guides. Demand and MC intersect near quantity 67 and price 27. ATC is U-shaped, reaching its minimum to the right of quantity 40. The 67 and 27 intersection values are approximate as labeled.

transcript.sourceText: The monopolist first finds output where MR = MC, which occurs at 40 units and a marginal value of $20. It then moves up to the demand curve, where buyers will pay $40 for 40 units. The profit-maximizing choice is therefore Q = 40 and P = $40, not the $20 MR value.
transcript.text: The monopolist first finds output where M R equals M C , which occurs at 40 units and a marginal value of 20 dollars . It then moves up to the demand curve, where buyers will pay 40 dollars for 40 units. The profit-maximizing choice is therefore Q equals 40 and P equals 40 dollars , not the 20 dollars MR value.

Find the output where MR crosses MC from above in the interior solution.
Move vertically from that output to the demand curve to find the monopoly price.

Do not set price equal to marginal revenue or marginal cost unless the graph happens to imply it.
A common mistake is to read monopoly price from the marginal-revenue curve. Find output where MR = MC, then read the price buyers will pay from demand.

The monopolist first finds output where MR = MC, which occurs at 40 units and a marginal value of $20. It then moves up to the demand curve, where buyers will pay $40 for 40 units. The profit-maximizing choice is therefore Q = 40 and P = $40, not the $20 MR value.
